---
title: "Disguise, Rotation, and Split-Field Coverage"
subtitle: "Why the defense you see before the snap is often not the defense you get, how safeties change the picture in the last half-second, and how one coverage can be two."
description: "Coverage disguise and post-snap rotation (two-high to one-high and back), the tells that leak through a disguise, late rotation and why it forces quarterbacks to read after the snap, split-field coverage and the 3x1 checks (poach, solo, stubbie), how offenses fight back with motion, tempo and hard counts, and how tracking data measures the lie."
glossary:
  Disguise: "Lining up in a way that hides or misrepresents the coverage (or pressure) the defense will actually play, so the quarterback's pre-snap read is wrong or useless."
  "Post-snap rotation": "Defenders, usually the safeties, moving at or just after the snap from the shell they showed into a different one: two-high into one-high, or one-high into two-high."
  "Late rotation": "A rotation timed to start at the snap or just after it, not during the cadence, so the quarterback gets no clean look at the real coverage before the play begins."
  "Split-field coverage": "Playing a different coverage on each half of the field (for example quarters to the wide side and Cover 2 to the short side), with each half following its own rules for the receivers on its side."
  "Cover 7 (match family)": "A label whose meaning depends on the staff. In Nick Saban's vocabulary it names a split-field, quarters-based pattern-match family built from a separate call for each side; other teams use 'Cover 7' for different coverages."
  Poach: "A check against a 3x1 formation in which the backside safety leaves the lone receiver to his cornerback and works across the field to take the trips side's inside receiver (#3) if he goes deep."
  "3x1 check (solo / stubbie)": {def: "A pre-planned adjustment of a two-high coverage to a 3x1 (trips) formation. In one common version of Solo the backside corner plays the lone receiver by himself and a linebacker takes #3 deep, freeing the backside safety; in Stubbie four defenders handle the three trips receivers and the backside safety stays home with the corner. Names and details vary by staff (some playbooks use 'Solo' for what this book calls poach).", aliases: ["Solo", "Stubbie"]}

`````` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (shared drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import os
import logging

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib.patches import RegularPolygon, FancyBboxPatch, FancyArrowPatch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Patch

from gridiron import Play, Player, offense, defense, routes as r, show_animation, style, draw_marker
from gridiron.play import MARKER_R

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
FPS = 10

# Predict-the-play answers: collapsed under each drill on the web, collected after Connections in print
ANSWERS = []


def answer(md):
    ANSWERS.append(md.strip())
    if PDF:
        print('\n*Answer: try it first, then see "Answers to Predict the play" at the end of the chapter.*\n')
    else:
        print('\n::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}\n\n' + md.strip() + "\n\n:::\n")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- alignments used all chapter
def nickel_vs_2x2(shell="two_high", safety_w=7.5):
    """11 personnel 2x2 against a nickel (4-2-5) defense. The Will apexes the left slot, the
    corners play 7 yards off, and two-high safeties sit 13 deep a few yards outside the hashes."""
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    dfn = defense("nickel", shell, off)
    out = []
    for p in dfn:
        if p.key == "WILL":
            p = p.moved(d=5.0, w=-6.0)
        elif p.pos == "CB":
            p = p.moved(d=7.0, w=p.w + (0.8 if p.w > 0 else -0.8), label="CB")
        elif p.key in ("FS", "SS") and shell == "two_high":
            p = p.moved(d=13.0, w=safety_w if p.w > 0 else -safety_w)
        out.append(p)
    return off, out


def protect(p, rushers=("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE")):
    """Five linemen set, four rushers engage them: enough to show it is a pass, no more."""
    for k in ("LT", "LG", "C", "RG", "RT"):
        p.block(k, pts=[(-1.2, 0.0)])
    for k in rushers:
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.6, 0.0)], speed=2.0)


def trips(detached=False):
    """11 personnel 3x1: X alone to the left; Z (#1), H (#2) and the tight end Y (#3) to the right.
    attached: Y in-line as the end on the line (a "trey" set). detached: Y flexed off the ball as a
    third slot and Z steps up to be the end on the line, so seven are still on the line."""
    off = offense("gun_trips")
    if detached:   # a real third slot: about 4 yards outside the tackle, a step off the ball
        off = [p.moved(d=-1.5, w=7.0) if p.key == "Y" else p.moved(d=-0.7) if p.key == "Z" else p
               for p in off]
    return off


def trips_defense(off, fs_w=-6.5):
    """Two-high nickel against 3x1. The backside corner presses X with a one-yard inside shade."""
    dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
    moves = {"FS": (12.0, fs_w), "SS": (12.0, 9.0), "LCB": (1.5, -14.0), "RCB": (7.0, 17.5),
             "NB": (5.0, 10.5), "MIKE": (4.5, 3.0), "WILL": (4.5, -2.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=moves[p.key][0], w=moves[p.key][1]) if p.key in moves else p for p in dfn]
    return [p.moved(label="CB") if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]


def number_receivers(p, d=-3.2, extra=None):
    """Label the trips receivers #1-#3 (outside in); `extra` adds a second label below, e.g. {"Y": "detached"}."""
    for key, txt in (("Z", "#1"), ("H", "#2"), ("Y", "#3")):
        pl = p.players[key]
        p.note(txt, at=(pl.d + d, pl.w))
        if extra and key in extra:
            p.note(extra[key], at=(pl.d + d - 1.8, pl.w - 1.0))


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Remove the painted yard-line numbers (they sit where wide receivers and safeties stand)."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_alpha() == 0.55:
            t.remove()


FIELD_W = 160 / 3


def ruler(fld, play, widths=False, fs=6.5):
    """Depth labels (yards past the line of scrimmage) down the left edge of the field window, so
    the faint 5-yard lines can be read as a scale. widths=True also marks where the hash marks and
    the painted numbers are, along the bottom edge. Drawn on the Field's ax: gridiron has no ruler."""
    ax = fld.ax
    x_left = FIELD_W - fld.y1 + 0.35                     # plot x of the window's left edge
    for d in range(5, 41, 5):
        y = play.los + d
        if fld.x0 + 0.8 <= y <= fld.x1 - 0.8:
            ax.text(x_left, y, f"{d}" + (" yd" if d == 5 else ""), fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2,
                    ha="left", va="center", zorder=12,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))
    if widths:
        y = fld.x0 + 0.9
        for yb, txt in ((23.58, "hash"), (FIELD_W - 23.58, "hash"), (13.0, "numbers"), (FIELD_W - 13.0, "numbers")):
            if fld.y0 + 1.5 <= yb <= fld.y1 - 1.5:
                ax.text(FIELD_W - yb, y, txt, fontsize=fs, color=style.INK_2, ha="center", va="center",
                        zorder=12, style="italic",
                        bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.85))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- two-time-state drawing
def ghost_marker(ax, x, y, label, ppy, color=style.DEFENSE):
    """A hollow, dashed defender: where he stood before the snap (the disguise)."""
    ax.add_patch(RegularPolygon((x, y), 4, radius=MARKER_R * 1.25, orientation=np.pi / 4,
                                facecolor="none", edgecolor=color, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)), zorder=6))
    if label:
        ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", color=color, fontweight="bold", zorder=6,
                fontsize=max(4.0, min(8.5, ppy * 0.75)))


def snapshot(play, t, ax=None, ghosts=(), ghost_t=None, lateral="full", window=(-8.5, 19.5),
             width_in=6.5, notes=(), show_ruler=False):
    """Everyone where he is at time t; `ghosts` also keep a hollow marker where they stood at
    `ghost_t` and a dashed trail from there, so the pre-snap picture survives in print."""
    pos = {k: play.position(k, t) for k in play.players}
    moved = [pl.moved(d=float(pos[k][0]), w=float(pos[k][1])) for k, pl in play.players.items()]
    q = Play([m for m in moved if m.side == "off"], [m for m in moved if m.side == "def"],
             los=play.los, ball_y=play.ball_y, to_go=play.to_go)
    q.highlights = dict(play.highlights)
    for n in notes:
        q.note(*n)
    fld = q.draw(ax=ax, lateral=lateral, window=window, width_in=width_in, title=False)
    ax, ppy = fld.ax, fld.pts_per_yard()
    no_numbers(ax)
    if show_ruler:
        ruler(fld, play, fs=5.5)
    P = lambda d, w: fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d, w))  # noqa: E731
    start = ghost_t if ghost_t is not None else play._compile()[1]
    for k, pl in play.players.items():
        if pl.side == "off" and pl.pos not in ("WR", "TE", "RB"):
            continue
        pts = np.array([play.position(k, tt) for tt in np.linspace(start, t, 30)])
        if np.ptp(pts[:, 0]) + np.ptp(pts[:, 1]) < 0.3:
            continue
        xs, ys = P(pts[:, 0], pts[:, 1])
        if pl.side == "off":
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.45, zorder=3)
        else:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), zorder=3)
    if ghost_t is not None and t > 0.05:
        for k in ghosts:
            x0, y0 = P(*play.position(k, ghost_t))
            ghost_marker(ax, float(x0), float(y0), play.players[k].label, ppy)
    bx, by = P(*play.ball_position(t))
    for kind, _, t_rel in getattr(play, "ball_events", []):
        if kind == "pass" and t > t_rel:          # a thrown ball: draw its flight so far
            sx, sy = P(*play.ball_position(t_rel))
            ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(sx), float(sy)), (float(bx), float(by)), arrowstyle="-|>",
                                         mutation_scale=8, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2, 1.5)), zorder=9))
    draw_marker(ax, float(bx), float(by), "ball", "", ppy)
    return fld


def strip(play, times, labels, ghosts=(), ghost_t=None, lateral=(-21, 21), window=(-8.5, 19.5),
          notes_at=None, width_in=6.5, ncols=2):
    """The print version of an animation: panels at chosen moments, ghosts kept on every
    post-snap panel so 'what was shown' and 'what was played' sit side by side."""
    n = len(times)
    nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
    pw = width_in / ncols
    h = nrows * (pw * (window[1] - window[0]) / abs(lateral[1] - lateral[0]) + 0.32)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, h), squeeze=False)
    for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
        ax.axis("off")
    for i, (ax, t, lab) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times, labels)):
        snapshot(play, t, ax=ax, ghosts=ghosts, ghost_t=ghost_t, lateral=lateral, window=window,
                 notes=(notes_at or {}).get(i, ()), show_ruler=(i == 0))
        ax.set_title(lab, fontsize=8.5, color=style.INK, loc="left")
    fig.tight_layout(h_pad=0.6, w_pad=0.4)
    h = [Patch(facecolor="none", edgecolor=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.2, ls=(0, (2, 1.2)),
               label="Dashed outline: where he stood before the snap (the disguise)"),
         Patch(facecolor=style.DEFENSE_TINT, edgecolor=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, label="Solid, filled: where he is now"),
         Line2D([], [], color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.3, ls=(0, (3, 2)), label="Defender's path"),
         Line2D([], [], color=style.OFFENSE, lw=1.0, alpha=0.6, label="Receiver's path")]
    fig.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 0.0), ncol=2, fontsize=7.5, frameon=False)
    return fig


def pointer(fld, play, text, text_at, to, ha="center"):
    """A labelled arrow from a text box to a spot on the field (both in (d, w) yards)."""
    tx, ty = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*text_at))
    px, py = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(*to))
    fld.ax.annotate(text, xy=(px, py), xytext=(tx, ty), ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=7.5, color=style.INK,
                    zorder=12, arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=style.INK_2, lw=0.9, shrinkB=7),
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))


def divider(fld, play, text_l, text_r, d_top=22.0, d_bot=-7.0):
    """A dashed line down the ball, captioning the two halves of a split-field call."""
    (x0, y0), (x1, y1) = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d_bot, 0.0)), fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d_top, 0.0))
    fld.ax.plot([x0, x1], [y0, y1], color=style.INK_2, lw=1.0, ls=(0, (6, 4)), zorder=2)
    for txt, ww, ha in ((text_l, -5.0, "right"), (text_r, 4.0, "left")):
        x, y = fld.xy(*play.to_abs(d_bot + 1.2, ww))
        fld.ax.text(x, y, txt, ha=ha, va="center", fontsize=8, color=style.INK, fontweight="bold", zorder=9,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.25", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, lw=0.6))
``````
:::


Third-and-7 from midfield. As the offense breaks the huddle, the broadcast's high camera shows
two safeties standing 13 yards deep, one on each side of the field, with a wide-open patch of
grass between them. The quarterback sees it too. Two deep safeties usually mean the deep middle
is empty, so he plans to throw a deep in-cut right into that patch. He takes the snap, sets his
feet, and lets it go, and a safety who had been standing 13 yards deep and 7 yards to the side
is suddenly sitting at 11 yards, right in the throwing lane. Interception. On the replay the
analyst circles both safeties and says "the coverage rotated." What does that mean? Why did one
safety sprint to the middle while the other one came forward? And if defenses can do that, why
does anyone bother to read the defense before the snap? This chapter is about the gap between
what a defense **shows** and what it **plays**, and about the last half-second in which that gap
closes.

**You'll be able to…**

- Say what a defense is doing when it disguises, and name the price it pays for it.
- Spot the common tells (safety depth and width, corner technique and leverage, weight and eyes,
  the timing of movement) and say before the snap which way a shell is likely to rotate.
- Call the two big rotations on the replay (and, with practice, live from the wide shot):
  two-high turning into one-high (often with a robber) and one-high turning into Cover 2.
- Recognise split-field coverage, read a Cover 6 call by its two halves, and explain how a defense
  answers a 3x1 formation with poach, solo or stubbie.
- Explain how offenses fight disguise with motion, tempo and hard counts, and why late rotation
  forces the quarterback to read after the snap.
- Read a tracking-data chart of safeties around the snap, and add *shell → rotation → leverage* to
  your pre-snap checklist.

::: {.callout-note title="You'll need"}
This chapter sits on top of the whole coverage part and a good deal before it. One line each:

- **Shells and the two families** ([A First Look at Defense](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-05-a-first-look-at-defense.qmd)):
  the [shell](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-shell-coverage-shell) is the safeties' picture
  before the snap: [one-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-one-high) (one deep safety in the
  middle) or [two-high](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-two-high) (two deep safeties, one per side).
  [Man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-coverage) means each defender has a receiver;
  [zone](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-zone-coverage) means each defender has an area.
- **Formations** ([Spread Formations](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-04-spread-and-modern-formations.qmd)):
  [2x2](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2x2) is two receivers on each side;
  [3x1](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x1) (trips) is three to one side and one to the other.
  Receivers are numbered from the sideline in: #1 is the widest on his side, then #2, then #3.
- **Motion** ([Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)):
  offenses move a player before the snap partly to make the defense react. A defender who
  [travels](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-travel-man-defender-follows-motion) with him suggests
  man; defenders who [bump](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bump-defensive-adjustment) over
  suggest zone; a safety who [spins](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spin-safety-rotation-on-motion)
  down suggests one-high. That is the [man/zone indicator](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-man-zone-indicator).
- **Cadence and checks** ([The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)):
  the quarterback can change the play at the line, and a
  [hard count](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hard-count) (a fake snap call) tries to make the
  defense move early.
- **Zones and the shell read** ([Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd)):
  deep zones are [thirds](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-third), [halves](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-half)
  or [quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-deep-quarter). Underneath, from the sideline in, are the
  [flat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-flat-zone) (near the sideline, 0–6 yards), the
  [curl](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-zone) (10–12 yards, between the numbers and the hash), the
  [hook](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hook-zone) (inside the curl, around the hash) and the
  [hole](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hole-zone) (the middle, 10–15 yards, in front of the deep
  safety). A defender's [landmark](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-landmark) is the spot his zone
  drop aims for. [Press](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-press)
  vs [off](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-off-coverage) corners and [bail](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bail)
  technique; [MOFC](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofc) (middle of the field closed, a deep
  safety in the middle) vs [MOFO](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mofo) (open, no one there);
  [pattern matching](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-pattern-matching) (zone defenders who pick up
  receivers who enter their area). The deep-middle spot is called the **post** (it is where a post
  route aims), so the safety who ends up there is the *post safety*, and "one safety in the post"
  means middle of the field closed. A corner in [trail technique](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-trail-technique)
  runs just behind and underneath his man, trusting a safety over the top.
- **Man coverage** ([Man Coverage](06-02-man-coverage.qmd)): [Cover 1](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-1)
  is man with one deep safety; [Cover 0](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0) is man with none; a
  [robber](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-robber) is a safety who sits in the hole 10–12 yards deep
  to undercut in-breaking routes; a [bracket](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bracket) puts two
  defenders on one receiver, one on each side.
- **Cover 3** ([Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd)): three deep, four under. It is usually reached by
  rotating a safety down: [sky](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-sky-rotation) (safety to the flat),
  [buzz](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-buzz-rotation) (safety to the curl) or
  [cloud](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cloud-rotation) (corner to the flat). The defender
  who covers both the curl and the flat on one side is the
  [curl-flat defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat-defender);
  [Cover 3 match](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-3-match) is Cover 3 whose zone players pick
  up receivers by pattern.
- **Cover 2** ([Cover 2 and Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd)): two deep halves, five under,
  with [hard corners](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hard-corner) who squat in the flats;
  [2-Man](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-2-man) is two deep with man underneath.
- **Quarters** ([Quarters and the Two-High Match Family](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd)):
  [quarters](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-quarters) gives four defenders a deep quarter each,
  with safeties who read #2 and fit the run; [Cover 6](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-6) is
  quarters on one side and Cover 2 on the other; [Palms](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-palms) is a
  two-high check in which the corner and safety on one side trade jobs on #1 and #2;
  [MEG](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-meg) means a corner plays his man everywhere he goes.
- **Routes and leverage** ([Passing Fundamentals](../04-the-passing-game/04-01-passing-fundamentals.qmd),
  [The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)): a [seam](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-seam)
  runs straight up between the hash and the numbers, a [post](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post)
  breaks deep toward the middle, a [dig](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dig) breaks flat inside at
  10–15 yards, an [out](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-out) breaks to the sideline, a
  [hitch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hitch) stops and turns back, and a
  [double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move) fakes one break and runs another. A
  defender's [leverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-leverage-inside-outside) is which side of
  the receiver he stands on: *inside* leverage protects the middle, *outside* the sideline.
- **Pass concepts and the quarterback** ([Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd),
  [Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd)): concepts like
  [dagger](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dagger) are built to beat a particular coverage, so the
  quarterback picks a side and a [progression](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-progression) (the
  order in which he looks at his receivers) partly from what he sees before the snap. When nothing
  is open he throws a short [checkdown](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-checkdown) to a back.
- **Run fits** ([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)):
  the number of defenders near the line versus the number of blockers decides whether a run has a
  chance, and a rotating safety is often the extra run defender.
- **Field landmarks** ([The Game in Fifteen Minutes](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd)):
  the NFL [hash marks](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hash-marks) sit only about 3 yards either
  side of the middle of the field, and the painted yard-line numbers start 12 yards in from each
  sideline, roughly 13 to 15 yards from the middle (sources in the split-field section). So "outside the hash" means 3 or more
  yards from the middle, and "on the numbers" means about 14 yards out, closer to the sideline than
  to the ball.
- **Who's who** ([The Twenty-Two](../01-foundations/01-03-the-twenty-two.qmd),
  [Formation Rules and Vocabulary](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd)):
  the [Mike](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-mike-linebacker) is the middle linebacker, the
  [Will](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-will-linebacker) the other (weak-side) linebacker in a
  nickel defense. On offense, [X](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-x-receiver) is the wide receiver on
  the line, [Z](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-z-receiver) the wide receiver off it,
  [Y](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-y-receiver) the tight end, and H the third wide receiver,
  usually in the slot. A *dropback* is a play on which the quarterback drops back to pass (sacks and
  scrambles included); coverage statistics are counted per dropback.

*Reading the diagrams:* offense is blue circles (X, Y, Z, H receivers; Q quarterback; R running
back; C center). Defense is outlined squares: E and T defensive ends and tackles, M the Mike, W the
Will, $ the nickel, CB a cornerback, FS and SS the free and strong safety. A **green ring** marks the
players to watch. The faint lines across the field are 5 yards apart, starting at the line of
scrimmage (the darker blue line), and the small numbers on the left edge give the depth in yards;
the short ticks are the hash marks. The orange line is the line to gain for that down. It moves
with the situation, so use the depth numbers, not the orange line, as your ruler. Dashed arrows are
defenders' movements, solid arrows receivers' routes, dotted lines man-coverage assignments.
:::

## Why a defense would lie

Start with what the quarterback is trying to do before the snap. In the 20 or so seconds he
spends at the line, he decides a lot: which way his linemen
[slide](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-slide-protection) in pass protection, which defender he
must throw away from if that defender blitzes, which side of the field his progression starts on, and whether the called play is any good against what he sees. If it
isn't, he can change it ([The Pre-Snap Phase](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd)).
Almost all of that depends on one question: **what coverage is this?** If he knows the coverage
before the snap, he knows roughly where the open grass will be before anyone has moved. Then the
play is half over before it starts.

The defense, meanwhile, has to put eleven people somewhere. And where they stand leaks
information, because of plain physics. A safety can only cover ground so fast. If he is going to
guard the deep middle of the field, he has to stand somewhere from which he can get there before
the ball does. If a cornerback is going to cover one receiver man-to-man, he tends to line up
facing that receiver, close to him, on the side he wants to protect. A defense that simply lined
up where its call works best would be handing the quarterback its call sheet.

**[Disguise](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-disguise)** is the answer: lining up in a way that
hides or misrepresents the coverage the defense will actually play. It comes in three flavours,
and good defenses use all of them:

1. **Show one thing, play another.** Line up in a two-high shell and play a one-high coverage, or
   the reverse. This is the dramatic kind, and the next three sections are about it.
2. **Show the same thing every time.** Line up in one shell for nearly everything, and play many
   coverages out of it. The quarterback isn't fooled so much as left without information. This is
   the quieter kind, and it is how the two-high defenses that spread through the NFL after 2018
   live. [Case Study: Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)
   tells that story in full.
3. **Move at the right moment.** Hold a picture until the last instant and change it at the snap,
   so there's no time to react. We'll call that late rotation below.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists"}
Disguise is about **time**. A quarterback who knows the coverage before the snap can decide where
to throw before the pass rush has started. A quarterback who must work it out after the snap
spends part of his roughly 2.5 to 3 seconds of protection just finding out what he is looking at.
The defense isn't trying to make the quarterback *wrong* so much as *late*. A late quarterback
holds the ball, takes sacks, throws into windows that close, or settles for a short checkdown.
:::

There's an asymmetry in the rules that makes this possible. The offense must be **set**: after a
shift, all eleven players have to be still for a full second before the snap, and only one player
may be in motion when the ball is snapped, and not toward the line. The defense has no such rule.
Defenders may move, shift, walk up and back out as much as they like before the snap, as long as
they stay out of the neutral zone (the strip, one ball long, between the two teams) and don't use words or acts meant to disconcert the offense at
the snap, such as imitating its snap count.[^rules] The offense has to hold still and be read, while the defense can keep moving.

### What disguise costs

- **The real job starts from the wrong spot.** A safety who shows two-high but is really the
  robber has to travel to his real landmark; one who shows one-high in the box and is really a
  deep-half player has a long way to run. Every yard of travel is time out of position.
- **The run defense gets worse.** A nickel defense usually has six or seven players near the line
  (four linemen, two linebackers, sometimes the nickel), the
  [box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box). A safety who comes down makes it seven or eight, but a
  safety standing 13 yards deep who is supposed to be that extra run defender arrives late. A safety walked down to look like a run defender
  who is really bailing to a deep half has left the box one man short. Offenses that run the ball
  well punish disguise by simply handing it off ([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)).
- **Communication and mistakes.** Every rotation is a little play inside the play, with its own
  timing and its own way to go wrong. When one safety rotates and the other doesn't, the defense
  ends up with two players in one zone and nobody in another: the "bust" you see when a receiver
  runs untouched through the middle of the field.
- **Practice time.** A defense that can play five coverages from one look has to rehearse all
  five from that look, and every extra starting look multiplies the reps. Something has to give.
  Some defenses keep one look and many coverages (flavour 2 above); others keep a short list of
  coverages and practise reaching each one from several looks (flavours 1 and 3). Few can afford
  both.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game the defense picks a play from a menu, and each defender walks to the spot that
play's diagram gives him. What you see is close to what was called. In the NFL, **alignment is a
separate decision from the call.** Coordinators design their calls so that several coverages
start from the same picture, and coach players to hold that picture until a set moment. Real
quarterbacks are taught to treat the pre-snap shell as a *hypothesis*, a best guess they expect
to confirm or overturn in the first second after the snap.
:::

## The physics of a disguise: what leaks before the snap

If you can't hide where you're going, you can at least make it hard to see. But the distances
involved put limits on what a defense can fake, and those limits are exactly what a good
quarterback (and now you) can read.

Some rough numbers. A deep pass is usually released around 3 seconds after the snap (in 2025 the
middle half of throws travelling 20 or more yards left between 2.6 and 3.6 seconds).[^ttt] But the
safety's real deadline is earlier: he has to be on top of the *receiver* before the receiver runs
past him, and in this chapter's simulated plays a slot receiver running up the seam is 15 yards
downfield about two seconds after the snap. The safety also can't sprint at the snap. His first
step or two are a read (is it a pass? where are the quarterback's eyes?), and a backpedal covers
ground noticeably more slowly than turning and running. The fastest safeties top out around 22
miles an hour, roughly 10 yards a second, but a safety reading the quarterback is rarely anywhere
near that.[^dbspeed]

So give him a working speed of 5 to 6.5 yards a second once he goes (the figure the simulated plays
use) and a few tenths of a second to read. That leaves about 1.6 seconds of running before the seam
receiver arrives: roughly **8 to 10 yards**. A safety 13 yards deep and 7.5 yards from the middle
(a few yards outside the hash) is about 8 yards from the deep-middle landmark at 16 or 17 yards:
inside the budget. One standing on the numbers, about 14 yards from the middle, is about 14 yards away:
far outside it.

Each defender's real job therefore draws a circle around his real
[landmark](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-landmark). He can line up anywhere inside it, and the
disguise has to fit inside every defender's circle at once. Within the circle there is still a
trade. A safety who will really be a robber at 10 or 11 yards can line up at 13 and still get there,
which keeps the two-high picture intact, but the trip costs him time. Lining up at 11 makes his job
easy, and it is also a tell. Every disguise is that bargain, made defender by defender: the closer to
the real job, the easier the job and the louder the tell. (These are model numbers for teaching the
idea, not measurements; with the real tracking data in
[Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
you can measure the circles.)

That is why disguises leak. Here is what to look at, and why each one tells you something. The
figure shows the textbook two-high spots as faint outlines so you can see how far each defender has
cheated from them.

::: {#cell-fig-tells .cell execution_count=2}
``` {.python .cell-code}

tell_moves = {"SS": (10.0, 5.0), "FS": (13.5, -5.5), "LCB": (1.2, -15.8), "RCB": (1.2, 15.8),
              "NB": (1.5, -8.2), "WILL": (4.5, 7.0)}
textbook = {k: (pl.d, pl.w) for k, pl in ((q.key, q) for q in dfn) if k in ("SS", "FS", "LCB", "RCB")}
dfn = [p.moved(d=tell_moves[p.key][0], w=tell_moves[p.key][1]) if p.key in tell_moves else p for p in dfn]
tells = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=7)
```

:::


- **Safety depth.** Deep-zone safeties in a two-high shell usually stand 12–14 yards off the
  ball. A safety at 8–10 yards is probably either coming down (into the box, the flat or the
  hole as a robber) or about to sprint backward, and the second is hard to do well. *Why it tells:*
  the deeper he is, the fewer underneath jobs he can reach in time; the shallower, the fewer deep
  ones.
- **Safety width.** A safety within about 8 yards of the middle (on the hash or a few yards
  outside it) can reach the deep middle. One splitting the hash and the numbers, 9 to 11 yards out,
  is probably staying on his half of the field. When one safety
  pinches toward the middle and the other widens or creeps down, the shell is leaning toward
  one-high. *Why:* the deep middle is a destination, and the safety who will go there likes to
  start close to it.
- **Corner technique, then leverage.** Two different questions. *Technique* (stance, eyes,
  depth) says man or zone: a man corner is square to his receiver with his eyes on him; a zone
  corner is turned toward the quarterback, seven or eight yards off and ready to backpedal or turn
  and run to a deep third, or five or six yards off and flat-footed (a squat Cover 2 corner). *Leverage* says
  where his help is. A corner who gives up the inside expects a safety or robber there (Cover 1,
  Cover 3). One who takes away the inside expects help over the top or has none (2-Man, Cover 0).
  *Why it tells:* the corner's technique has to match his job, and technique is hard to fake.
  Corners can disguise too: a corner pressed in a two-high look who bails at the snap, one who
  shows deep-third depth and comes up into the flat (the cloud rotation), or a corner and safety who
  trade jobs (an *invert*: the safety comes down to the flat and the corner bails to the deep half,
  as Palms does on one side). They have less room to lie than safeties do, but an invert means the
  deep player can be a corner, so on the replay watch the two *deepest* defenders, whoever they are.
- **Eyes and weight.** Zone defenders look at the quarterback. Man defenders look at their man.
  A safety leaning forward on his toes is thinking about coming downhill; one sitting on his heels
  is thinking about getting depth. This is the hardest tell to see on a broadcast, but the
  All-22 film coaches use (a high, wide camera showing all 22 players) shows it.
- **Timing.** When does anyone move? A safety who drifts toward his real spot during the cadence
  (coaches say he *creeps* or *walks down*) is giving away his rotation; one who stands still until
  the ball moves is not. That discipline has a name, late rotation, and its own section below.
- **Situation and tendency.** A defense that always rotates to the field on third-and-long has a
  habit opponents will have found on film
  ([Tendencies](../13-analytics-and-data/13-04-tendencies-proe-and-charting.qmd)). The best
  disguises also break the defense's own patterns.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"Two high safeties means Cover 2." It doesn't. Two-high is a **shell**, a picture, not a
coverage. From the same two-high look a defense can play Cover 2, 2-Man, quarters, Cover 6 or
Palms, or rotate into Cover 3 or Cover 1 at the snap. What the shell tells you is which coverages
are *easy* from here, and so which ones are likely. To name the coverage, look again one second
after the snap.
:::

## Post-snap rotation, part 1: two-high becomes one-high

**[Post-snap rotation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-post-snap-rotation)** is defenders
(almost always the safeties) moving at the snap from the shell they showed into a different one.
The most common version starts two-high and ends one-high: one safety races to the deep middle and
the other comes down. Where the down safety lands decides the coverage. If he goes to the flat,
it's a sky rotation into Cover 3. To the curl area, a buzz rotation. To the hole in the middle
of the field at 10 or 11 yards, it's Cover 3 or Cover 1 with a robber. In Cover 3 robber the
robber is one of the four underneath defenders: the two curl-flat players and the hook player
keep their zones and the robber takes the hole in front of the deep safety. (You'll also hear
[rat](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-rat): some staffs use it for any robber, others only for a
linebacker sitting in the low hole at 5 to 8 yards, as in "Cover 1 rat".)
([Cover 3](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) built all three from a one-high start; here they start
from two.)

Coaches describe all this movement with a pile of short verbs, and some of them mean different
things in different mouths. This chapter uses them like this:

| Word | What the defender does |
|:-------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|
| *rotate*, *spin* | The whole shell turns: one safety goes to the post, the other comes down. "He spun down" and "he spun to the post" are both used; the verb names the rotation, not the direction. |
| *come down*, *drop down* | A deep safety moves toward the line, into the box, the flat, the curl or the hole. |
| *bail* | A defender who looked shallow turns and runs to a deep zone at the snap. |
| *sink* | A defender gives ground a few yards straight back, keeping his eyes forward. |
| *creep*, *walk down*, *cheat* | Small moves toward the real job *before* the snap; they are tells. |
| *rob* | Sit in a throwing lane (usually the hole) and jump in-breaking routes. |
| *poach* | A backside safety leaves his side to help on the trips side (see below). |

::: {#cell-fig-rotate-to-robber .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def rob_play():
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=55, to_go=7)
    # pre-snap: nobody in the secondary moves. The Mike's tiny shuffle only gives the play
    # pre-snap frames to draw (gridiron starts the clock at the first pre-snap movement).
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.6), speed=0.12)
    # offense: dagger to the right (the seam clears out, the dig comes in behind it)
    p.route("Y", r.path((12, -1.0), (20, -2.0))); p.route("Z", r.dig(12, 11)); p.route("X", r.go(20))
    p.route("H", r.hitch(5)); p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    p.pass_to("Z", t=1.7)
    protect(p)
    # defense: four rush; the rest rotate to Cover 3 with a robber
    p.drop("FS", (16.5, 0.0), speed=6.5)
    p.drop("SS", (11.0, 4.0), speed=4.5)
    # the boundary corner keeps his cushion on X's go route; the field corner squeezes over the dig
    p.drop("LCB", (20.5, -16.0), speed=5.5); p.drop("RCB", (15.0, 15.5))
    p.drop("NB", (6.5, 12.0)); p.drop("WILL", (6.5, -11.0)); p.drop("MIKE", (7.0, -2.0))
    p.highlight("FS", "SS")
    return p


rob = rob_play()
ROB_T = [-1.4, 0.0, 1.0, 2.6]
if PDF:
    strip(rob, ROB_T, ["−1.4 s · Two-high, as shown", "Snap · nothing has moved",
                       "+1.0 s · FS to the post, SS comes down", "+2.6 s · Cover 3 robber: the dig is thrown into him"],
          ghosts=("FS", "SS"), ghost_t=-1.4, window=(-8.5, 23.0),
          notes_at={3: [("robber", (13.4, 8.6)), ("deep middle", (20.2, -4.5))]})
    plt.show()
else:
    show_animation(rob, times=ROB_T)
```

Two-high rotates to Cover 3 with a robber. Before the snap (panel 1) both safeties sit 13 yards deep, one on each side: the deep middle looks open. Panels 1 and 2 are identical, and that is the point: no defensive back moves until the ball does. At the snap the free safety (FS) runs to the deep middle while the strong safety (SS) comes down and in to the hole at about 11 yards, right where Z's dig is heading; the ball (panel 4) is thrown into him. The dashed outlines show where the safeties stood before the snap. The corners turn and run to deep thirds (the left one stays on top of X's go route); underneath, the Will and the nickel ($) take the curl-flat zones, the Mike the hook and the SS the hole. In print, the four panels are four moments of one play.
:::
:::


Follow the play from the quarterback's side. Before the snap he sees two-high and an empty deep
middle. Against two-high, the space between the safeties and behind the linebackers is often
where the ball should go, and [dagger](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-dagger) (a seam route that
pulls the underneath and deep defenders away, with a deep dig coming in behind it; see
[Dropback Concepts](../04-the-passing-game/04-04-dropback-concepts.qmd)) is built to hit it. Here
Y's seam bends slightly inside to push the middle open. At the snap, the defense changes the
answer. The free safety's sprint to the middle puts a defender over the top of the seam. The strong safety's short trip down and in puts
him exactly where the dig is going to arrive. The quarterback who decided before the snap, and
throws on time without looking, throws it to the robber.

Notice the distances. The free safety travels about 8 yards to the deep middle, inside the 8-to-10
yard circle from the previous section. That's possible only because he lined up 7 or 8 yards from
the middle, not on the numbers. The strong safety travels about 4 yards. Neither had far to go, which is the whole design. The shell was two-high, but
each safety was standing where his *real* job was still within reach.

The same rotation can land in man coverage instead: Cover 1 robber. The safeties move exactly as
they do here, so the difference is in the corners. In Cover 3 they turn and run to deep thirds with
their eyes on the quarterback; in Cover 1 they stay on their receivers, pressing or trailing them
wherever they go. One second after the snap, the corners tell you which.

What beats the robber, once the quarterback sees him? The throws he left behind. He has come down
from one side, so the seam and the curl on that side are thinner, and his spot in the hole is in
front of the deep safety, so a route that gets *behind* him (a post or deep crosser) is open if the
post safety is late. The rest of Cover 3's weaknesses are still there too: the seams between
the deep middle and each deep third, and four underneath defenders who can't cover every short
zone, so stress the curl-flat defender on the far side with a route in front of him and one behind. [Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)
builds the quarterback's side of this.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: two-high to one-high"}
**What it solves.** It gets an extra defender near the line against the run, or a robber
against in-breaking routes, without announcing either before the snap. Offenses facing two-high
tend to run the ball, because with both safeties 12 or more yards deep only six or seven defenders
are near the line to face the offense's blockers, and to throw between the safeties. The rotation punishes
both: the down safety adds a run defender or sits in the throwing lane.

**What it gives up.** The rotating safety starts late and from deep, so he arrives in the box
after the run has started. The safety spinning to the middle has a long run, so a quick deep
throw outside him (a post or a deep corner route released before he gets there) can beat it.
And the robber looks only at the quarterback, so a quarterback who looks him off with his eyes and
shoulders, then throws elsewhere, can move him out of the play
([Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)).
:::

### Which safety comes down? A rule, not a whim

A defense doesn't decide on the field which safety rotates. The call says so, usually by tying the
rotation to something the offense shows: rotate **to the passing strength** (the side with more
receivers), **to the field** (the wide side), **toward motion**, or the other way, **weak** or **to
the boundary**. Staffs build names for these out of a direction and a landing spot ("sky strong,"
"buzz weak" and the like); one of Nick Saban's trips calls, for example, drops the safety down to
the passing strength.[^saban7] Before the snap, then, your best guess about direction is:

- **Toward the strength or the motion** is the default. That is where the extra receivers are,
  so that is where an extra underneath defender helps most. Quarterbacks are taught to expect it.
- **Away from the strength** is itself a disguise. A defense that knows the quarterback expects
  the strong safety to come down can spin the weak safety down instead, so the robber appears on
  the side the quarterback thought was clean.
- **Look for the tells on one safety, not both.** The safety who is shallower, narrower or leaning
  forward is the likely down safety; the other one is the likely post safety. Combine that with
  the strength of the formation and you can usually call the direction.

## Post-snap rotation, part 2: one-high becomes two-high

The rotation can run the other way. Show one-high: a single safety deep in the middle, the
other safety walked down near the box, corners off and ready to bail, the classic Cover 3 or
Cover 1 picture. Then, at the snap, the deep safety bails to one deep half and the down safety
bails to the other. The corners, instead of bailing to deep thirds, hold their depth and widen
into the flats, the Cover 2 corner's job. That is
Cover 2 (or, with man coverage underneath, 2-Man), reached from a one-high start.

::: {#cell-fig-spin-to-two .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def spin_play():
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2("single_high")
    dfn = [p.moved(d=13.5, w=0.0) if p.key == "FS" else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(d=9.0, w=6.0) if p.key == "SS" else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(d=8.0) if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=55, to_go=7)
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.6), speed=0.12)      # pre-snap frames only; the secondary stays still
    # offense: outs outside (good against one-high with off corners), seams inside
    p.route("X", r.out(8, 5)); p.route("Z", r.out(8, 5)); p.route("H", r.seam(20))
    p.route("Y", r.path((10, 0.0), (19, -5.0)))            # a seam that bends into the open middle
    p.route("RB", r.flat(1.5, 6), side=-1)
    p.dropback(2.5)
    protect(p)
```

One-high bails to Cover 2. Before the snap the free safety (FS) is alone in the deep middle and the strong safety (SS) is down at 9 yards: middle of the field closed. Panels 1 and 2 are the same picture: no defensive back moves before the snap. At the snap both safeties bail to deep halves, landing between the hash and the numbers, and the corners (CB), who looked as though they would bail to deep thirds, hold their depth and widen three yards toward the sideline (compare each corner with his dashed outline). That puts them right where the outside receivers' 8-yard outs are breaking. They play the flat from on top, at about 8 yards rather than the flat's usual 0 to 6, because a corner who starts deep keeps the out in front of him. What opened is the deep middle between the two safeties: H's seam holds the left safety, and Y bends his route inside into the open middle.
:::
:::


Why bother? One-high with off corners *invites* certain throws. With a safety in the deep middle
and the corners backing off, the outside is where the quarterback looks: quick outs and hitches
in front of the bailing corners, curls under them, back-shoulder throws to receivers facing
one-on-one coverage. The bail to Cover 2 takes all of that away at once. The corners now sit
exactly where the outs are going, and there's a safety over the top on each side to take away
the deep ball outside.

What opens instead is the deep middle, between the two safeties, which is exactly what the
quarterback ruled out before the snap. A quarterback who reads the safeties *after* the snap sees
them split and throws between them, up the seam or on a post (the throw that
[Cover 2 and Tampa 2](06-04-cover-2-and-tampa-2.qmd) shows the Tampa 2 Mike running to carry). The
other Cover 2 window is the sideline [hole shot](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hole-shot), the
gap behind the corner and in front of the half-field safety, 18 to 22 yards deep. A quarterback
who decided before the snap throws the out into a waiting corner.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: one-high to two-high"}
**What it solves.** It lets a defense look like it is loading up against the run, with the down
safety near the box, and still play two deep defenders against the pass. Offenses that see
one-high often check to throws outside or to deep shots against single (one-on-one) coverage. The
bail punishes both.

**What it gives up.** The down safety was a run defender in the picture, and now he's running
away from the line, so a run against this look faces one fewer defender than it seemed to. He also
has the longest trip on the field, 8 or more yards of depth plus width, so a fast vertical route
outside can reach his area before he does.
:::

## Late rotation: winning the last half-second

The two plays above have something in common. In both, nothing moves until the snap. That is
the difference between a rotation the quarterback can see and one he can't.

**[Late rotation](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-late-rotation)** means timing the rotation to
start at the snap or just after it, rather than during the cadence. A defense that rotates early
(safeties drifting into place while the quarterback calls signals) gives him a free look: he sees
the real coverage, still has time to change the play, and the disguise has bought nothing. A
defense that rotates late shows him the real coverage only after the play has begun. He has to
recognise it *while* dropping back, with the pass rush coming.

It is also why late rotation is risky. A safety who starts moving at the snap is a step behind one
who was already there, so the rotation has to be fast and the distances have to be short. Every
late rotation is a race between the safety and the first throw.

The clearest way to see a rotation is to track just the two safeties, how deep each one is and
how far from the middle, frame by frame from three seconds before the snap to two seconds after.
Player-tracking data records exactly that: every player's position ten times a second, from chips
in the shoulder pads. The figure below is built from simulated plays written out in the format of
the NFL's [Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
tracking files (that chapter builds it step by step from the real files).

::: {#916d6d0b .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (simulated BDB-format tracking used by the next two figures)"}
def _seg(p, key, start, end, tau, speed):
    """Move `key` from start to end at `speed`, starting at time tau (negative = before the snap)."""
    start, end = np.array(start, float), np.array(end, float)
    L = float(np.linalg.norm(end - start))
    if tau < 0:                                  # part of the trip happens before the snap
        pre = min(L, speed * -tau)
        mid = start + (end - start) * (pre / L if L else 0)
        p.motion(key, to=tuple(mid), speed=max(pre / -tau, 0.05))
        if L - pre > 0.05:
            p.drop(key, tuple(end), speed=speed)
    else:
        p.drop(key, tuple(end), speed=speed, delay=tau)


def sim_play(kind, rng, tau=None, play_id=0):
    """One simulated dropback, returned as Big Data Bowl-style tracking rows (10 frames a second).

    kind: 'stay2' (two-high shown and played), 'rot1' (two-high shown, rotated to one-high),
          'stay1' (one-high shown and played), 'spin2' (one-high shown, bailed to two-high).
    tau : when the safeties start their post-snap move (seconds; negative = before the snap).
    """
    off, dfn = nickel_vs_2x2()
    side = rng.choice([-1, 1])
    if kind in ("stay2", "rot1"):
        d1, d2 = rng.uniform(11.5, 14.0, 2)
        w1, w2 = rng.uniform(5.5, 8.5, 2)
        fs0, ss0 = (d1, -side * w1), (d2, side * w2)
    else:
        fs0 = (rng.uniform(13.0, 15.5), rng.uniform(-1.5, 1.5))
        ss0 = (rng.uniform(7.0, 10.0), side * rng.uniform(4.0, 7.0))
    dfn = [q.moved(d=fs0[0], w=fs0[1]) if q.key == "FS" else q for q in dfn]
    dfn = [q.moved(d=ss0[0], w=ss0[1]) if q.key == "SS" else q for q in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
    p.motion("MIKE", to=(4.5, 1.5), speed=0.1)   # a slow 3-second shuffle so frames start 3 s early
    p.route("X", r.go(22)); p.route("Z", r.go(22)); p.route("H", r.seam(20)); p.route("Y", r.seam(20))
    p.dropback(2.5)
    tau = rng.uniform(-0.9, 0.3) if tau is None else tau
    v = rng.uniform(5.0, 6.5)
    if kind == "stay2":
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (fs0[0] + rng.uniform(2, 4), fs0[1] - side * rng.uniform(0.5, 2.5)), max(tau, 0), v * .6)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (ss0[0] + rng.uniform(2, 4), ss0[1] + side * rng.uniform(0.5, 2.5)), max(tau, 0), v * .6)
    elif kind == "rot1":
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (rng.uniform(15.5, 18.0), rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0)), tau, v)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (rng.uniform(8.0, 10.5), side * rng.uniform(3.0, 6.0)), tau, v * 0.8)
    elif kind == "stay1":
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (fs0[0] + rng.uniform(2, 4), fs0[1]), max(tau, 0), v * 0.6)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (ss0[0] + rng.uniform(-1, 1), ss0[1] + side * rng.uniform(1, 4)), max(tau, 0), v * 0.6)
    else:
        _seg(p, "FS", fs0, (rng.uniform(15.5, 18.0), -side * rng.uniform(9.0, 12.0)), tau, v)
        _seg(p, "SS", ss0, (rng.uniform(15.5, 18.0), side * rng.uniform(9.0, 12.0)), tau, v)
    trk = p.to_tracking(fps=FPS, play_id=play_id)   # columns: gameId, playId, nflId, frameId, x, y, s, a, ...
    trk["kind"], trk["los"], trk["ball_y"] = kind, p.los, p.ball_y
    return trk


def shell_at(frame, deep=10.0, split=3.5):
    """Classify one frame of any BDB-style play: 'two-high' if two or more defenders are 10+ yards
    deep and none of them is within 3.5 yards (sideways) of the ball; otherwise 'one-high'.
    Meant for pre-snap frames only: after the snap, a corner bailing past 10 yards would count."""
    dfn = frame[frame["side"] == "def"]
    d = dfn["x"] - frame["los"].iloc[0]
    w = (frame["ball_y"].iloc[0] - dfn["y"]).abs()
    deep_w = w[d >= deep]
    return "two-high" if len(deep_w) >= 2 and deep_w.min() >= split else "one-high"
```

Read it as a picture of the idea, not as evidence: the simulation only plays back the timings we
gave it. What it shows is the shape to look for. A rotation is a *divergence*: before it starts,
the rotated plays and the honest plays are indistinguishable, and within about ten frames (one
second) the safeties are in completely different places. When the divergence starts before the
snap, even by half a second, the quarterback still has time to use it: he can change the
protection, check to another play, or decide which side his progression starts on. A defense
coached for late rotation pushes that starting point to zero or past it. (In these simulated plays
the ball sits in the middle of the field, so "sideways from the middle" is also sideways from the
ball. With the ball on a hash the two differ by about 3 yards, and coaches set the post safety's
landmark by one or the other depending on the system.)

Real safeties won't look this tidy. They shuffle, bounce on their toes, take false steps and
adjust to motion, so real tracking lines are noisier and the plays are far less alike. We haven't
checked these simulated paths against real tracking; the chapter on tracking data does that with
the real files.

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (the same figure from real Big Data Bowl 2025 files; not run here)"}
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb

# BDB 2025: 2022 season, Weeks 1-9, with pre-snap frames. Files from Kaggle (login required).
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")          # has pff_passCoverage, absoluteYardlineNumber
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")

frames = []
# One bdb.prepare() call per play is slow over nine weeks (minutes, not seconds). For speed, group
# the tracking by (gameId, playId) once and prepare each group; this loop is written for clarity.
for (g, pl), _ in plays.groupby(["gameId", "playId"]):
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=g, play_id=pl)   # offense moving +x, time 0 = snap
    ball = one[(one["side"] == "ball") & (one["frameType"] == "SNAP")]
    los, ball_y = float(ball["x"].iloc[0]), float(ball["y"].iloc[0])
    one["frame_rel"] = (one["time"] * 10).round().astype(int)
    # "Safeties" = the two deepest defenders one second before the snap, not roster FS/SS:
    # teams play three-safety nickel, and corners rotate to the post in cloud or invert calls.
    pre = one[(one["side"] == "def") & (one["frame_rel"] == -10)]
    ids = pre.nlargest(2, "x")["nflId"]
    s = one[one["nflId"].isin(ids)].copy()
    s["depth"] = s["x"] - los
    s["from_middle"] = (s["y"] - ball_y).abs()             # sideways from the ball, as in the simulation
    frames.append(s[s["frame_rel"].between(-30, 20)].assign(gameId=g, playId=pl))
saf = pd.concat(frames).merge(plays[["gameId", "playId", "pff_passCoverage"]], on=["gameId", "playId"])
# ...then label each safety's role and plot exactly as in the simulated figure above.
```

## Split-field coverage: two halves, two answers

So far the whole defense has rotated together. A different idea, and one of the most important in
modern defense, is to **not treat the field as one problem at all**.

**[Split-field coverage](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-split-field-coverage)** means playing a
different coverage on each half of the field, with each half following its own rules for the
receivers on its side. The split is usually made one of two ways: by **formation** (the side with
more receivers, the *strong* side, against the side with fewer) or by **field position** (the
[field side](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-side), the wider side of the field when the
ball sits on a hash mark, against the [boundary side](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-boundary-side),
the shorter one).

You have already met the most common split-field coverage: [Cover 6](06-05-quarters-and-match.qmd),
quarters on one half and Cover 2 on the other. Here it is with the split made by field position:
the ball is on the left hash, so the field (wide) side is to the offense's right.

::: {#cell-fig-cover6-split .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def cover6():
    off = offense("gun_2x2")
    # ball on the left hash: the field-side receivers split wider, Z to the field numbers
    off = [p.moved(w=18.0) if p.key == "Z" else p.moved(w=11.0) if p.key == "Y" else p for p in off]
    dfn = defense("nickel", "two_high", off)
    moves = {"WILL": (5.0, -6.0), "RCB": (7.0, 18.8), "LCB": (5.0, -16.0), "FS": (12.5, -7.5),
             "SS": (12.5, 8.5), "NB": (5.0, 11.0)}
    dfn = [p.moved(d=moves[p.key][0], w=moves[p.key][1]) if p.key in moves else p for p in dfn]
    dfn = [p.moved(label="CB") if p.pos == "CB" else p for p in dfn]
    p = Play(off, dfn, los=45, ball_y="left", to_go=10)
    # field side: quarters
    p.drop("RCB", (15.0, 17.0), speed=4.0); p.zone((17.0, 15.5), (8, 11), "¼")
    p.drop("SS", (15.0, 6.0), speed=4.0); p.zone((17.0, 5.0), (8, 10), "¼")
    p.drop("NB", (5.5, 12.5)); p.zone((6.0, 14.0), (5, 7), "curl-flat")
    # boundary side: Cover 2 (the half-field safety owns everything from the sideline to the middle)
    p.drop("FS", (15.5, -9.0)); p.zone((17.5, -9.0), (8, 17), "½")
    p.drop("LCB", (5.5, -17.0)); p.zone((4.0, -18.5), (4.5, 6), "flat")
    p.drop("WILL", (7.0, -7.5)); p.zone((7.5, -9.5), (4.5, 6), "curl")
    p.drop("MIKE", (6.5, 3.0)); p.zone((7.5, 3.2), (4.5, 5.5), "hook")
    for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
        p.rush(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
    p.highlight("LCB", "RCB")
    return p
```

Why split the field? Because the two halves really are different problems.

- **The field and the boundary are different sizes, a little.** NFL hash marks sit 70 feet 9
  inches from each sideline, so with the ball on a hash there are about 23.6 yards to the near
  (boundary) sideline and 29.7 to the far (field) one, a difference of about 6 yards. In college
  the hashes are 60 feet from the sidelines, so the split is about 20 yards against 33.[^hashes] A
  boundary corner has the sideline as an extra defender; he can squat in the flat because a throw
  over his head has little room to land. That difference is big in college, which is where
  field/boundary quarters grew up. In the NFL it is modest, which is one reason pro split-field
  calls are often keyed to the formation's **strength** (the trips side, the tight-end side)
  rather than to the field.
- **The two halves face different receivers.** A tight end and a slot to one side, a lone
  wideout to the other: those sides threaten different things, and one coverage rule can't be
  ideal for both.
- **Each player's job is simpler.** Each player only has to know his own half: who is #1 and #2
  on my side, and what is my rule against them? The defense gets flexibility from combining simple
  halves, not from teaching eleven people one complicated call. The defenders in the middle, the
  Mike and the hook players, belong to whichever half the call assigns them; in the figure above
  the Mike takes the hook in the middle, the Will the curl for the Cover 2 half and the nickel the
  curl-flat for the quarters half.
- **But the communication is harder.** Both halves have to agree where the split is: by
  formation, by field, or, with the ball in the middle and a balanced formation, by a default the
  staff sets in advance. A safety or the Mike typically makes that strength call by shout and hand
  signal. When a receiver motions across the formation, the strength can flip, and both halves
  must re-declare in the last second before the snap. That is a big reason offenses motion so much
  against split-field defenses (see below).

Split-field coverage is also a disguise machine, and that's why it belongs in this chapter. From
one two-high alignment the defense can play quarters on both halves, Cover 2 on both, Cover 6 to
either side, Palms on one side, or rotate to one-high. The quarterback now has to read *two*
coverages, one per half. A pre-snap guess that is right about the left half can be wrong about
the right.

How do you tell Cover 6 from its neighbours after the snap? Count the deep safeties first, then
watch the corners. Cover 3: one safety in the deep middle, both corners bail. Cover 2: two
safeties split the field, both corners sit down in the flats. Cover 6: two safeties split the
field, and the corners *disagree*: one sits in the flat (the Cover 2 half), the other backpedals
with his eyes on the quarterback and plays a deep quarter. One squatting corner and one bailing
corner under two deep safeties is the Cover 6 picture.

One naming warning before the history. Coverage numbers are dialect, not law
([Coverage Fundamentals](06-01-coverage-fundamentals.qmd) and the dialect table in the
[coverage atlas](../../appendices/appendix-d-coverage-pressure-atlas.qmd)), and "Cover 7" is the
clearest example. In Nick Saban's vocabulary,
**[Cover 7](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-7-match-family)** names a whole *family*: a
two-high, quarters-based pattern-match coverage in which each side of the formation gets its own
small call, so the full call is a split-field call assembled from parts.[^cover7] Other staffs use
"Cover 7" for a man-match coverage, a bracket on one receiver, or nothing at all.

### A short history: from college laboratories to the NFL

Split-field quarters grew up in college football in the 1990s and 2000s, and the problem it solved
is easy to state. College offenses spread the field and ran option and play-action from the same
looks, on wide college hashes. A defense that put a safety in the box to stop the run gave up the
deep ball; one that kept both safeties deep got run over. Quarters let it have both: safeties at
10 to 12 yards who read the receivers in front of them and fit the run if it came, but stayed deep
if it was a pass. TCU's Gary Patterson, one of the coaches most identified with the approach,
summed up the safeties' job at a 2015 coaches' clinic: "Don't go till you know." His safeties didn't
backpedal at the snap; they shuffled flat-footed and read, because, as he told the same clinic
audience, "we want to take away the short game, we want to take away combination routes, and we
want to stop the run."[^patterson]

Saban's pattern-matching quarters, which goes back to his years as Bill Belichick's defensive
coordinator in Cleveland (1991 to 1994), went with him to Michigan State, LSU and Alabama. Michigan
State under Mark Dantonio and Pat Narduzzi, Patterson's TCU and Iowa's long-running quarters
defenses became reference points that other coaches studied at clinics.[^quartershistory]

The NFL caught up later, and fast. NFL Next Gen Stats (NGS, the league's tracking-data arm)
measures how often defenses play a split-safety (two-high) coverage after the snap: 32.9% of
dropbacks in 2018, 37.8% in 2021, 40.4% in 2024 and 42.0% in 2025, the highest since tracking
began. In 2025, Cover 6 alone was 9.2% of coverages.[^ngs-two-high] Brandon Staley's 2020 Rams
(below) are one of the teams that made the approach fashionable in the league. Staley came from the
staff of Vic Fangio, the defensive coordinator most associated with the NFL's two-high wave, and
coaches from Staley's staff and Fangio's wider tree, such as Ejiro Evero (the Rams' safeties coach in 2020, then Denver's
defensive coordinator in 2022 and Carolina's since 2023), have leaned on rotation from a two-high
shell: by one count, Carolina stayed two-high and rotated to one-high in almost equal measure.[^evero] The
full story of the two-high spread, Vic Fangio and the counterpunch that followed, is told in
[Case Study: Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd)
and [The Modern Era](../11-history/11-05-the-modern-era.qmd).

## Trips: the formation that forces a decision

Split-field rules work beautifully against 2x2: two receivers and two or three defenders per
side. A **3x1** formation (trips) breaks the symmetry on purpose. Three receivers go to one side
and one to the other, and now the count is ugly.

Count only the players who can run with a receiver 20 yards downfield. On the trips side the
defense has the corner, the safety and the nickel against three receivers who can all go deep. On
the backside it has a corner and a safety against one receiver. (The backside linebacker, the Will,
is there too, but his jobs are the run and a short zone; he can't chase a receiver up the field.)
If the defense just plays quarters as usual, the trouble is the third receiver (#3, the one closest
to the ball). Quarters rules are built for two receivers per side: the corner takes #1 deep and the
safety reads #2. Most systems do give #3 to someone underneath, the hook or [apex](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-apex) player who walls
him off (stays in his path and keeps him from running free across the middle). But if #2 and #3
*both* run vertical, the safety can carry only one of them, and the underneath defender can't
carry a fast receiver 20 yards deep. Meanwhile two defenders on the backside guard one man.
Offenses love this: send #2 and #3 vertical and see who covers the second one. The problem is
sharpest when #3 is a *detached* receiver, a slot or a tight end split off the line, who can get
up the field fast; an in-line tight end is slower to release, and many quarters teams just play
their normal rules against him.

So every two-high defense carries a set of **3x1 checks**: pre-planned adjustments that tell
each player what to do when trips appears. They fall into a few families. All of them answer the
same question: *who takes #3 if he goes deep, and who gets left alone because of it?*

### Poach: the backside safety comes across

**[Poach](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-poach)** is the most aggressive answer. The backside
safety ignores the lone receiver, leaves him to the cornerback in pure man coverage, and works
across the field to take #3 if #3 runs deep. The trips side can then play its normal quarters
rules on #1 and #2.

::: {#cell-fig-poach .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
off = trips(detached=True)
dfn = trips_defense(off)
dfn = [p.moved(d=5.0, w=-13.8) if p.key == "LCB" else p for p in dfn]
poach = Play(off, dfn, los=35, to_go=10)
poach.route("Z", r.go(20)); poach.route("H", r.seam(20)); poach.route("Y", r.path((4, -1.0), (20, -2.5)))
poach.route("X", r.fade(18))
for k in ("SDE", "SDT", "WDT", "WDE"):
    poach.rush(k, pts=[(-1.4, 0.0)], speed=2.0)
poach.drop("FS", (17.0, 3.0)); poach.drop("SS", (17.0, 10.5)); poach.drop("RCB", (17.0, 18.5))
poach.drop("NB", (6.5, 14.0)); poach.drop("MIKE", (7.0, 5.0)); poach.drop("WILL", (7.0, -4.5))
poach.man("LCB", "X")
poach.note("poach: FS takes #3 deep", at=(20.0, -7.0))
poach.note("CB alone on X", at=(6.0, -19.0))
number_receivers(poach, extra={"Y": "Y detached"})
poach.highlight("FS")
fld = poach.draw(lateral="full", window=(-8, 22))

plt.show()
```

Poach is a *read*, not a man assignment. If #3 goes vertical, the poaching safety carries him. If
#3 stays short or breaks outside, the safety doesn't stand around: he robs inside, jumping #2's
in-breaking route or the backside dig, or works back to help on X. That is what separates poach
from a backside safety simply locked on #3 in man coverage.

The trade is stated in the picture. Poach turns the trips side into a fair fight and gives the
defense a deep player over #3, but the corner on the backside is now on an island. Offenses who
expect poach build "poach beaters": they put their best receiver alone on the backside (often
called an *X-iso* look) and attack him knowing no safety is coming, or they attack the poaching
safety himself with a route that breaks behind him as he runs to #3.[^poachbeater] The poaching safety's alignment is also a tell: a backside
safety who starts closer to the middle than usual, or who leans toward the trips side, is
probably not staying home.

### Solo and stubbie: other ways to solve the count

The **[3x1 check (solo / stubbie)](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-3x1-check-solo-stubbie)** family
covers the other common answers. The names are shared across many playbooks but the details
aren't, so treat these as the typical versions rather than the only ones.

**Solo.** A warning first: if you search for "solo coverage", most of what you'll find, from pro
and big-college quarters writers, uses *Solo* for the backside corner alone on X while the backside
*safety* takes #3 vertical. That is the call this chapter has just shown you as poach. The version
here comes from other playbooks, and we keep it under the name solo because it is a genuinely
different answer, with a different defender on #3: the backside corner plays the single receiver by
himself, and a linebacker, usually the Mike, takes #3 if he runs deep. That frees the backside
safety to be an extra run defender against trips runs and run-pass options.[^solo] *The trade:* a linebacker running with a tight end or slot up the seam is a mismatch the
offense will look for, which is why NFL defenses rarely ask a linebacker to carry a *detached* #3
deep. Solo shows up mostly against tight-end trips, where #3 is in-line and slower to get going.

::: {#cell-fig-solo .cell execution_count=10}

``` {.python .cell-code}
solo = Play(off, trips_defense(off), los=35, to_go=None)

solo.man("LCB", "X"); solo.man("MIKE", "Y")
solo.drop("MIKE", (12.0, 3.5)); solo.drop("FS", (5.5, -4.0))

fld = solo.draw(lateral=(-20, 21), window=(-6.5, 16.5), title=False)
```

**Stubbie.** Instead of sending help across, the defense solves trips on the trips side alone,
four defenders against three receivers. In the version taught in Saban's system (as decoded in
Cameron Soran's guide to Saban's coverages, cited above) the corner plays #1 man-to-man wherever he
goes, the nickel takes #2, a linebacker walls off #3 underneath, and the safety takes #3 deep while
staying over the top of #2. He can do both because he lines up deeper than either and between them:
if #3 goes vertical he carries him, and if #3 stays short he sits over #2, helping the nickel on
anything deep. The backside safety stays home, so the lone receiver faces two defenders. *The
trade:* the trips-side corner is locked in man coverage, and those four players are spread thin
against crossing routes.
