**Rotate.** The defense can also give up on two-high against trips and rotate to a one-high,
three-deep [Cover 3 match](06-03-cover-3-family.qmd) coverage, with the trips-side safety coming
down toward the passing strength and the backside safety becoming the deep-middle player.

Why does this matter to a viewer? Because **trips is how offenses force the defense to declare.**
The 3x1 check the defense uses usually shows up in the backside safety's alignment before the
snap: home and wide (stubbie), cheated in toward the middle (poach, or a rotation in which he
becomes the post safety), or creeping down (solo). Poach and rotation can look the same before
the snap; the difference shows in the first second after it. The poaching safety keeps reading #3
and goes where #3 goes; the rotating safety runs to the deep middle and stays there, while the
trips-side safety comes down. And offenses use motion to *create* trips at the last moment, so the
defense has to make that decision with a second left on the play clock. Usually a safety or the
Mike shouts and signals the check. A defender who doesn't hear it plays the old call, and that is
how the busts described at the start of the chapter happen: two defenders on one receiver, nobody
on #3.

The same question comes up against other three-receiver sides. An [empty](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-empty)
3x2 set has a trips side too, and the defense answers it with the same families. A [bunch](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-bunch), three
receivers packed tightly together, adds a different problem, receivers crossing each other at the
line, which [Man Coverage](06-02-man-coverage.qmd) handles with its
[banjo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-banjo) calls.

## How offenses fight back

Offenses' counters share one idea: **make the defense show its hand earlier, or make the hand
not matter.**

**Motion.** Moving a receiver before the snap forces defenders to adjust, and adjustments are
information ([Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd)).
A cornerback who travels across the formation with the motion man hints at man coverage. A
safety who spins down hints at one-high. Motion also changes the receiver count: turning 2x2 into
3x1 forces the defense into its trips check with no time to disguise it. The league has gone
all in. PFF (Pro Football Focus, a charting and grading company) counted pre-snap shifts or
motion on 63.9% of plays in 2025, up from 43.0% in 2018.[^pff-motion]

Defenses answer motion in three ways:

- **Match rules.** In a pattern-match zone, defenders hand receivers off by rule, so a defender
  may follow the motion man a few steps (looking like man) and then pass him to the next zone. The
  motion read says "man" and the coverage is zone, or the reverse.
- **Fake spins.** A safety spins down with the motion on purpose and goes back to his old job at
  the snap.
- **Many starting points.** The defense rehearses every rotation from more than one pre-snap
  picture, so no single picture means one coverage.

The offense's counter to all three is [motion at the snap](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-motion-at-the-snap):
the receiver is still moving when the ball is snapped, so the defense must react to him and rotate
at the same instant, with no time for a second move.

**Tempo.** Snapping the ball quickly gives the defense less time to line up, communicate and
disguise. Under [tempo](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tempo) (the pace at which an offense gets
to the line and snaps the ball; see
[In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd)),
defenses often fall back on one simple call, and simple calls are easier to read.

**Hard counts.** A hard count isn't only fishing for an offside flag. Safeties drilled to move "on
the snap" sometimes move on what *sounds* like the snap, and a safety who flinches at a fake
reveals where he's going. The defense's answer is discipline: key the ball, not the voice.

**Read it after the snap.** The deepest answer is for the quarterback to stop relying on the
pre-snap picture. Modern quarterbacks are taught to form a pre-snap guess, then confirm it in the
first steps of the drop by looking at the safeties: is the middle of the field closed or open
*now*? Which safety moved, and where? Pass concepts are built to have an answer against either
rotation. The classic example is a slot receiver on a "bender" in four verticals: if the middle
opens (two safeties split), he bends his seam into a post between them (see
[four verticals](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-four-verticals)), as Y does in the Cover 2
figure above; if the middle closes (one safety in the post), he stays on his seam and the ball goes
away from the post safety. The route changes after the snap, on the same read the quarterback
makes. Eye manipulation, looking off a robber to move him, is the advanced version
([Concepts Versus Coverages](../08-the-chess-match/08-01-concepts-versus-coverages.qmd)).

**Play-action and RPOs.** The safety who rotates down is usually the defense's extra run
defender, and that makes him a target. A [run-pass option](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd)
can *read* him: if he comes down to fit the run, throw where he left; if he stays deep, hand off
into a box that is one defender short. [Play-action](../04-the-passing-game/04-05-play-action-boots-screens.qmd)
attacks the other safety: a run fake holds the post safety's eyes for a beat, and his long trip to
the middle is exactly the kind of run a deep shot behind him is built to beat. Rotation buys the
defense a run defender it never announced; a good run fake makes it pay for him.

**Throw before it matters.** The quick game (throws out in about two seconds or less;
[The Quick Game](../04-the-passing-game/04-03-quick-game.qmd)) doesn't care much about
rotations, because the ball is gone before the safeties have finished moving. Against heavy
disguise, a steady diet of quick throws is a way of declining the contest.

## Measuring the lie

Can you count how often a defense lies? Broadcasters and charting services label the coverage
*after* the snap, and the nflverse data used throughout this course carries those labels
(2018–2025). What they don't record is the picture the defense showed *before* the snap. For that
you need tracking data: the safeties' positions in the frames before the snap.

That is exactly what the 2025 Big Data Bowl asked for. Its theme was pre-snap behaviour, and it was
the first edition whose tracking files included full pre-snap frames, from the first nine weeks of
the 2022 season. The winning entry, by NYU students Smit Bajaj and Vishakh Sandwar, was called
"Exposing Coverage Tells in the Pre-Snap."[^bdb2025] NFL Next Gen Stats then built a pre-snap
model of its own, crediting that project as inspiration. It classifies the shell a quarterback
sees before the snap and compares it with the coverage after. In its words: "If a defense shows
split-safety zone and rotates to single-high man (or spins to Cover 0), we flag it as
disguised."[^ngs-disguise] The article that introduced the model gave no league-wide disguise
rate, we found no other published one, and the Big Data Bowl files cover only half of one season.
So "how often does an NFL defense lie?" has no public league-wide answer yet (one analyst's count
for a single team is in the Film room below).

Here is how you would get one. First fix what "the shell" means: the picture once the offense is
set and the quarterback starts his cadence, say two seconds before the snap. Then classify that
picture with a simple rule (two or more defenders at least 10 yards deep and none of them near the
middle means two-high), do the same at the snap, and compare both with the coverage the defense
actually played. A defense that rotates during the cadence has still disguised, but the
quarterback had time to see the truth; one that rotates at the snap did not give him that time.

The chart below runs that measurement on eight **made-up** defenses. We typed in how often each one
disguises and how late it moves, simulated 90 plays for each as BDB-format tracking, and let the
classifier score them, so the chart can only give back what we put in. Its job is to show what the
measurement looks like and how to read it, not to tell you anything about real teams. Read each row
from left to right: the hollow dot is how often the picture two seconds before the snap told the
truth, the filled dot how often the picture at the snap did, and the bar between them is how much of
the lie the defense gave away during the cadence.

::: {#cell-fig-shell-agreement .cell execution_count=12}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
# hypothetical defenses: (share shown two-high, share disguised, share of disguises that move only at/after the snap)
DEFS = {"A": (0.50, 0.05, 0.5), "B": (0.55, 0.12, 0.4), "C": (0.45, 0.25, 0.1), "D": (0.60, 0.30, 0.2),
        "E": (0.65, 0.30, 0.5), "F": (0.70, 0.35, 0.9), "G": (0.75, 0.40, 0.6), "H": (0.75, 0.45, 0.9)}
N = 90
res, pid = [], 0
for name, (p_two, p_dis, p_late) in DEFS.items():
    n_dis = round(N * p_dis)
    for i in range(N):
        pid += 1
        shown_two = rng.random() < p_two
        disguised, late = i < n_dis, i < round(n_dis * p_late)
        kind = {(True, False): "stay2", (True, True): "rot1",
                (False, False): "stay1", (False, True): "spin2"}[(shown_two, disguised)]
        tau = rng.uniform(0.0, 0.3) if late else rng.uniform(-1.6, -0.6)
        trk = sim_play(kind, rng, tau=tau, play_id=pid)
        played = "two-high" if kind in ("stay2", "spin2") else "one-high"   # the post-snap label
        res.append((name, played,
                    shell_at(trk[np.isclose(trk["time"], -2.0)]),
                    shell_at(trk[np.isclose(trk["time"], 0.0)])))
chk = pd.DataFrame(res, columns=["defense", "played", "shell_early", "shell_snap"])
agree = (chk.assign(early=chk["shell_early"] == chk["played"], snap=chk["shell_snap"] == chk["played"])
            .groupby("defense")[["early", "snap"]].mean().mul(100))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 3.6))
y = np.arange(len(agree))[::-1]                   # Defense A at the top
ax.hlines(y, agree["early"], agree["snap"], color=style.BASELINE, lw=2.0, zorder=1)
ax.scatter(agree["early"], y, s=46, facecolor="white", edgecolor=style.SERIES[0], lw=1.6, zorder=2,
           label="2 seconds before the snap")
ax.scatter(agree["snap"], y, s=46, color=style.SERIES[0], zorder=3, label="at the snap")
ax.set_yticks(y, [f"Defense {d}" for d in agree.index], fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Plays where the pre-snap shell matched the coverage played (%)", fontsize=8.5)
ax.set_xlim(50, 101)
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
ax.legend(loc="lower right", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Pre-snap shell vs coverage played (simulated defenses, BDB-format)", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Two numbers, then, describe a defense's disguise: *how often* it lies sets how low its early
score can go, and *when* it moves decides whether the lie can be caught in time. With the real 2025
Big Data Bowl files, whose plays carry a charted post-snap coverage, the same code would give real
values; the website's "Show the Python" holds it, and
[Tracking Data and the Big Data Bowl](../13-analytics-and-data/13-05-tracking-data-and-big-data-bowl.qmd)
runs it on real defenses.

::: {#c226723b .cell execution_count=13}
``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (the real version from Big Data Bowl 2025 files; not run here)"}
from gridiron import bdb

plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")        # pff_passCoverage is the post-snap label
trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")
TWO_HIGH = {"Cover-2", "2-Man", "Quarters", "Cover-6 Right", "Cover 6-Left"}   # check the year's label list
ONE_HIGH = {"Cover-1", "Cover-3", "Cover-3 Seam", "Cover-3 Cloud Left", "Cover-3 Cloud Right",
            "Cover-3 Double Cloud", "Cover-1 Double", "Cover-0"}

out = []
for row in plays.dropna(subset=["pff_passCoverage"]).itertuples():
    one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=row.gameId, play_id=row.playId)
    snap = one[one["frameType"] == "SNAP"]
    one["los"] = float(snap.loc[snap["side"] == "ball", "x"].iloc[0])
    one["ball_y"] = float(snap.loc[snap["side"] == "ball", "y"].iloc[0])
    played = ("two-high" if row.pff_passCoverage in TWO_HIGH
              else "one-high" if row.pff_passCoverage in ONE_HIGH else None)
    if played is None:
        continue
    out.append((row.defensiveTeam, played,
                shell_at(one[np.isclose(one["time"], -2.0)]), shell_at(one[np.isclose(one["time"], 0.0)])))
# ...then group by defensiveTeam and plot exactly as in the simulated chart above.
```

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Vikings 2023–2025 — Brian Flores and the defense that is both"}
Brian Flores became the Vikings' defensive coordinator in 2023 and was still there in 2026. His
defenses have been described as close to unreadable before the snap. The back seven (the
linebackers and defensive backs, everyone behind the defensive line) move constantly, safeties
change the shell during the cadence and again at the snap, and pressure comes from players who
don't look like rushers. In 2023 the Vikings blitzed on 50.7% of opponents' dropbacks, the highest
rate in the league. After a 23–17 Vikings win in Week 2 of 2024, 49ers quarterback Brock Purdy told
Flores on the field, "The scheme, man, it's crazy."[^vikings-cbs]

**What to notice:** CBS's breakdown of that 49ers game shows the two halves of the trick. On one
snap six Vikings stand on the line before the snap and the play becomes a four-man rush with seven
in coverage. On another, a blitz look is real but the coverage behind it is split-field
Cover 6 (both plays are in the same CBS piece). Watch the number of defenders at the
line before the snap, then count the rushers after it. With Flores, the two numbers often differ.

What makes it work is the **spread of possibilities** behind one look. In the nflverse post-snap
coverage labels for 2023–2025, the Vikings played two-high coverage more often than any other
defense (51.4% of charted dropbacks, just ahead of Buffalo's 50.5%) and Cover 0, man with no deep
safety, at 5.8%, behind only Kansas City and level with Baltimore; the Chiefs under Steve Spagnuolo
sit right beside them on both counts. The chart shows the menu, not the disguise: post-snap

defenses a quarterback who sees two-high can lean on the odds that it stays two-high; against a
defense that lives at both ends, the odds are no help. (The blitz numbers are pressure disguise,

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Rams 2020 — Brandon Staley's first year"}
Brandon Staley arrived in Los Angeles in 2020 as a first-time NFL defensive coordinator, from Vic
Fangio's staff in Denver, and took over a defense with two great individual players: Aaron
Donald inside and Jalen Ramsey at cornerback. He built it around a two-high shell. Most snaps
looked alike before the snap, and the coverage was decided at and after it: quarters and Cover 6
to the field or the boundary, rotations down into Cover 3 or a robber, and Ramsey moved around
the formation, from outside corner to the nickel ("star") spot, to follow the matchup.[^ringer]
Three things made the light-box, two-high approach affordable. Donald's four-man pass rush meant
the Rams didn't need to blitz more than an average defense (they sent five or more rushers on about
a quarter of dropbacks, close to the league median). The front, with Donald inside, could hold up
against the run with fewer defenders in the box, while the safeties fitted the run from depth
([Run Fits and Box Math](../05-defensive-fronts-and-run-defense/05-05-run-fits-and-box-math.qmd)).
And the defense was disciplined enough to rotate late.

**What to notice:** on a 2020 Rams passing down, find Ramsey first (outside or in the slot), then
the two safeties: level and deep while the quarterback calls signals, with the rotation, if there
is one, coming only as the ball moves. The results: the 2020 Rams finished the regular season first
in the NFL in points allowed (18.6 a game), total yards allowed (281.9) and passing yards allowed
(190.7).[^rams2020] Staley was hired as the Chargers' head coach after one season, and the Rams'
approach spread through his coaching tree and the league. Its parent, Fangio's system, is the subject of
[Case Study: Fangio's Two-High Revolution and Macdonald's Answer](../12-case-studies/12-08-two-high-to-macdonald.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Panthers under Ejiro Evero — the coin-flip rotation"}
Ejiro Evero, a safeties coach on Staley's 2020 Rams staff, has run Carolina's defense since 2023.
His Panthers are the cleanest public example of this chapter's main move: show two-high, then
decide at the snap whether to stay there or rotate a safety down to a single-high, "closed-post"
coverage. In Cody Alexander's charting of the Panthers' defense, published in April 2026, they
stayed two-high 397 times and rotated 375 times, what he called "an almost perfect
1:1 ratio." Cornerback Jaycee Horn described what that felt like from inside: "Everything is really
out of a shell, not many tells or pre(-snap) things. It was just on the snap; everything
happened."[^panthers]

**What to notice:** on a Carolina passing down, call the shell as the quarterback starts his
cadence; it will almost always be two-high. Then, on the replay, watch the two safeties at the snap.
Roughly half the time one of them comes down and the other runs to the middle; the rest of the time
both stay deep. Nothing before the snap tells you which, and that is the design. It also gives you a
benchmark for your own log below: one charted NFL defense built around disguise rotated out of its
two-high shell on about half the snaps that started there.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it on Sunday: call it twice"}
For one quarter (two if you're keen), on every obvious passing down, make two calls out loud and
write them down.

- **Call 1, as the quarterback starts his cadence: the shell.** One-high or two-high? Then the
  details that could change it: how deep is each safety, is one narrower or shallower, are the
  corners pressed or off? Which side is the formation's strength?
- **Call 2, one second after the snap: what it became.** Is the middle of the field closed (one
  safety in the post) or open (two safeties splitting the field)? Closed: Cover 1 if the corners
  turn and run with receivers, Cover 3 if they bail into deep thirds. Open: then the corners tell
  you which, squatting in the flats for Cover 2 (or that side of Cover 6), backpedalling with eyes
  on the quarterback for quarters, trailing their man for 2-Man. No safety deep at all: Cover 0.
  If the two safeties went to two different jobs, notice which one came down and where he landed.
- **Log the lie.** Mark each play S (same) or R (rotated). By the end of the quarter you'll have
  a *disguise rate* for that defense. For scale, the Panthers in the film room above rotated out of
  two-high on about half their two-high snaps. Also note whether the rotation started *before* the snap
  (you could see it coming) or *at* the snap (you couldn't). Both count as a lie; only the second
  one worked.
- **Bonus: trips.** When the offense shows 3x1, watch the backside safety. Did he stay home
  (stubbie), come across to #3 (poach), run to the deep middle (rotate), or come down (solo)?
  Then watch where the ball went.

Live, Call 1 needs a shot that shows the safeties: the wide pre-snap view some broadcasts use while
the quarterback surveys the defense, or a high camera behind the offense. The standard live angle
sits at the line and often cuts the safeties out of frame at the snap, so on many plays Call 1 has
to wait for the replay. The high, wide replays (the closest a broadcast gets to the
[All-22](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-all-22) film coaches use) are the best place to check
yourself: use the first replay to see the shell and the second to check the rotation.
:::

**What will the shell turn into at the snap, and which side of the field should the quarterback
be wary of?**

``` {.python .cell-code}
answer(r"""
**Most likely a rotation to one-high zone, Cover 3, with the right safety (SS) coming down.**
The safety tells: the SS has crept to 10 yards and stands 5 yards from the middle, while the FS is
at 13.5 and 7 yards out. The SS is shallower and narrower, so he can reach the curl or the hole
quickly, and he has crept down as the play clock runs out (a timing tell). The FS is the deeper
one and can reach the deep middle. The corner tells: they are 8 yards off, outside and turned to
the quarterback, which is zone technique, the way deep-third corners line up, not the square,
pressed stance of man corners. You can't tell before the snap whether the SS will land in the curl
(a **buzz** rotation) or in the hole (a robber), and you don't need to: either way he lands in the
in-breaking lanes on the right.

For the quarterback, the danger is to the **right**: curls and digs on that side run straight into
the SS. The opportunities are the classic Cover 3 ones away from the rotation, such as stressing
the left [curl-flat defender](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-curl-flat-defender) with a curl-and-flat
combination, or the seam on the left between the deep middle and the deep third (the Cover 3
weaknesses listed with the robber rotation). Of course a disciplined defense could show exactly this and
stay two-high.
""")
```

**Which 3x1 check does this look like, and where would you throw?**

``` {.python .cell-code}
answer(r"""
**Poach, or a rotation; either way, X is alone.** The left (backside) safety is only about 4 yards
from the middle, much narrower than the right safety at 9. A backside safety staying home to help
on X would be wider and square to X, so he isn't home: he is getting ready to go somewhere on the
trips side. Before the snap there are two candidates. In **poach** he reads #3 and carries him if
he goes up the middle. In a **rotation** to one-high he becomes the deep-middle safety and the
trips-side safety comes down. The clue here is that the right safety is still deep and wide, not
creeping down, which leans toward poach, but you confirm it after the snap: the poacher goes where
#3 goes; the rotating safety runs to the middle and stays there. The left corner fits both. He is
pressed a yard inside X (inside leverage), taking away the inside, which is what a corner does when
he expects no help over the top.

**Throw to X**, especially if X is the offense's best receiver. Against poach, X is one-on-one with no help. The classic poach beaters are a
[back-shoulder](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-back-shoulder-throw) fade or a go route outside (the corner gave up the outside to take away the inside),
or a [double move](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-double-move). Against the rotation, X still
faces his corner with the post safety starting far away. It's also worth sending #3 vertical
anyway, so the safety has to commit.
""")
```

**What did the motion tell the offense? And what could the defense still do to it at the snap, and
how would the offense take that away?**

``` {.python .cell-code}
answer(r"""
**It suggested one-high zone, Cover 3 rotating toward the motion.** Nobody went with Z across the
formation, and the right corner stayed home over empty grass: a corner with no man to cover is
playing a zone, here a deep third. The left safety coming down toward the motion while the right
safety rotates to the post is the defense moving to a single deep safety, with the FS as an
underneath (buzz or sky) defender on the side Z is going to. That is the
[spin](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spin-safety-rotation-on-motion) from
[Motion and Shifts as Weapons](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-06-motion-and-shifts.qmd), and it
goes the default way: toward the motion, which is where the receivers now are.

**The catch:** a defense that knows you use motion to read it can spin on purpose and then rotate
*back* at the snap. That is late rotation used against the motion read, and it's a favourite of
heavy-disguise defenses. The offense's counter is in the timing: snapping the ball as Z passes the
quarterback (motion at the snap) leaves the safeties almost no time to re-rotate, so the picture
they show during the motion is much more likely to be the real one. It is still a strong hint, not
a certainty.
""")
```

## Checklist so far (Parts 1–6)

Part 6 ends here, so it's time to update the pre-snap card. The lines this part of the book exists
for are **shell → rotation → leverage**. Read them in that order: the shell gives you a
first guess, the rotation (or its absence) confirms or overturns it, and the corners finish the
read: their technique (eyes, stance, depth) tells you man or zone, and their leverage tells you
where the help is.

## Takeaways

- **The shell is a hypothesis, not an answer.** Defenses choose their alignment separately from
  their coverage, and the best ones show the same picture for many calls. Name the shell before
  the snap, and expect to check it one second after.
- **Disguise buys time, and it costs something.** Every defender must line up where his real job
  is still reachable, so disguises leak: safety depth and width, corner technique and leverage,
  eyes, and above all the *timing* of movement. Late rotation hides the most and risks the most.
  Which safety rotates is set by the call, most often toward the strength or the motion.
- **Rotations run both ways.** Two-high can become Cover 3 or a robber (taking away the middle
  throws two-high invites); one-high can bail into Cover 2 (taking away the outside throws
  one-high invites). Each rotation opens the area the quarterback ruled out.
- **Split-field coverage plays two coverages at once,** one per half, keyed to strong and weak
  or (more in college, with its wide hashes) field and boundary. Each player's job is simpler; the
  communication is harder, and motion across the split tests it. It is a big part of why two-high
  defenses spread through the NFL after 2018.
- **Trips forces a decision,** and the decision is about #3: the backside safety comes across
  (poach), a linebacker takes him (solo), the trips side handles it four-on-three (stubbie), or
  the defense rotates. Whoever is left alone is where the offense will attack.
- **Offenses answer by forcing the defense to show earlier or by making the picture not matter:**
  motion, tempo, hard counts, post-snap reads, play-action and RPOs that target the rotating
  safety, and quick throws.
